india_specific_finding: PARTIAL. Tretinoin (retinoic acid and its salts) is explicitly PROHIBITED as a cosmetic ingredient -- listed at Annex A (GNRAS/prohibited list) Serial No. 375 of IS 4707 (Part 2):2017, which is incorporated into Cosmetics Rules 2020 by reference via Rule 39(2). This matches EU/US practice where retinoic acid is prescription-only, not a cosmetic. However, the actual cosmetic-grade forms used in this project's scope -- Retinol, Retinyl Palmitate, Retinyl Acetate -- do NOT appear in Annex A (prohibited) or Annex B (restricted-with-conditions) of the verified 2017 text, so no India-specific concentration cap exists for them; EU limits (0.3% face / 0.05% body per Reg 2024/996) or US/CIR guidance apply by default. CAVEAT: BIS gazetted a 5th revision, IS 4707 (Part 2):2025, on 21 Aug 2025, mandatory from 9 Feb 2026, which may have added a retinol-specific entry mirroring the EU's 2024 change -- the 2025 full text could not be accessed for free to confirm or rule this out, so treat as an open item, not a finding.

YES -- confirmed India-specific concentration limit, actively enforced. Rule 39 of Cosmetics Rules 2020, read with Annex B Serial No. 98 of IS 4707 (Part 2):2017, caps salicylic acid at 2.0% in leave-on/other cosmetic products and 3.0% in rinse-off hair products (not to be used in products for children under 3 except shampoos); a separate 0.5% cap applies when it is used specifically as a preservative (Annex C, Serial No. 4). The numeric limits mirror EU Annex III/V, but the rule is independently codified in Indian law and was actively enforced: on 20 May 2025 the Drugs Controller General (India) cancelled the import registration of 7 Mesoestetic/Dermamelan products (importer: Spectra Medical India Pvt Ltd) for containing 7-30% salicylic acid, citing Rule 39 and Annex B Serial No. 98 by name.

YES, and it is a significant divergence. Under Annex B (restricted-with-conditions) Serial No. 94 of IS 4707 (Part 2):2017, benzoyl peroxide's ONLY authorized cosmetic use is in artificial nail systems, capped at 0.7% (after mixing), professional use only. It is not on the authorized-use list for general leave-on acne/face-care use at any concentration -- this mirrors the EU (Annex III), where BP acne products are treated as medicines, not cosmetics, not the US (FDA OTC drug monograph permits 2.5-10% for acne). Practical implication for this project: a benzoyl-peroxide acne face wash/spot-gel does not have a codified 'safe cosmetic concentration' under Indian law the way it does under the US FDA monograph -- such a product sits outside the cosmetic standard entirely. Note real-world caveat: enforcement against BP face products appears inconsistent (many are sold OTC as cosmetics in Indian retail today), so this is a gap between the codified BIS standard and observed market practice -- worth flagging to the team as a judgment call, not a settled fact.

YES -- two independent India-specific restrictions, stricter than the US. (1) IS 4707 (Part 2):2017 Annex A (prohibited list) Serial No. 1333 prohibits hydroquinone as a hair-dye substance; Amendment 1:2017 narrows the wording to 'prohibited except for the use in Annex B entry 16' (a narrow nail-hardener-adjacent technical use) -- skin-lightening/depigmenting use is NOT an authorized use anywhere in Annex B, so hydroquinone is not permitted as a general cosmetic skin-lightening active. (2) Separately, under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945, hydroquinone-containing preparations were added to the Note under Schedule H (prescription-only drugs) via Notification G.S.R. 186(E) dated 6 March 2019, in force from 1 April 2019 -- this ended OTC sale of hydroquinone skin-lightening products; they may only be sold as a Schedule H prescription drug through a pharmacy. (The G.S.R. number is reported consistently across multiple independent secondary legal-update sources; it was not independently re-fetched from egazette.gov.in in this pass.) Net effect: stricter than the US (FDA permits OTC hydroquinone up to 2%) and comparable to the EU (hydroquinone banned in cosmetics since 2000/2001, hair-dye/nail exceptions aside).

NO INDIA-SPECIFIC RULE FOUND. Searched the full text of IS 4707 (Part 2):2017 -- Annex A (prohibited/GNRAS), Annex B (restricted-with-conditions), Annex C (preservatives), Annex D (UV filters) -- 'kojic acid' does not appear in any of them. No CDSCO gazette notification, circular, or public notice referencing kojic acid was found either. EU/US rules apply by default: EU capped kojic acid at 1% (skin-lightening use, face/hand products) via Regulation (EU) 2024/996, effective from Nov 2025; India's verified 2017 standard predates that change. CAVEAT: BIS's 5th revision (IS 4707 Part 2:2025, mandatory from 9 Feb 2026) was not accessible for free verification and may have added a matching entry -- flagged as an open item, not confirmed either way.

NO INDIA-SPECIFIC RULE FOUND. 'Arbutin' does not appear anywhere in IS 4707 (Part 2):2017 Annexes A-D (prohibited, restricted, preservatives, UV filters), and no CDSCO notice referencing arbutin was found. EU/US rules apply by default: EU added alpha-arbutin and arbutin to Annex III via Regulation (EU) 2024/996 -- alpha-arbutin capped at 2% in face creams / 0.5% in body lotions, arbutin at 7% in face creams, effective from Nov 2025. Same pending-revision caveat as Kojic Acid: IS 4707 (Part 2):2025 (mandatory Feb 2026) was not independently verified and may or may not have added an equivalent entry.

NO INDIA-SPECIFIC RULE FOUND. 'Glycolic' does not appear anywhere in IS 4707 (Part 2):2017 Annexes A-D, and no BIS standard or CDSCO notice restricting glycolic acid or AHAs as a class was located. This is consistent with global practice, not a gap unique to India: even EU/US treatment of AHAs is mostly guidance rather than a hard binding cap (EU SCCS opinion suggests ~4% at pH >= 3.8 for glycolic acid, but this is not a binding EU Annex III entry; US FDA guidance on AHA labeling is a labeling recommendation, not a concentration cap). India simply has no additional layer here -- defer to whatever EU/US/CIR guidance this project already uses for AHAs.

YES -- India has two of its own sunscreen-specific standards, distinct from EU/US frameworks. (1) IS 4707 (Part 4):2022, 'List of U.V. Filters Allowed in Cosmetics with Restriction' -- India's own positive list of permitted UV-filter actives with concentration caps, structured like (and largely aligned to) the EU's Annex VI UV-filter list; confirmed to exist via BIS's official standard-details portal, though the ingredient-by-ingredient text was not independently pulled in this pass. (2) IS 17494 -- 'Cosmetics: Sun Protection Test Methods, In-vivo Determination of SPF' (ISO 24444-aligned), originally published 2021, revised and reissued as IS 17494:2025 (superseding the 2021 edition 24 Sep 2025). Multiple independent industry/press sources report BIS/CDSCO is making in-vivo SPF testing MANDATORY for SPF label claims from 10 January 2026, ending reliance on in-vitro/mathematical SPF estimation -- this was NOT independently confirmed against a primary BIS/PIB/gazette document in this pass (secondary sources only), so treat the specific mandatory-date claim as needing verification before it is hard-coded into the chatbot, even though the standard's existence and revision history are real. This is a big, very current development for this project to flag regardless -- it affects every sunscreen SKU's label claim, independent of any single active ingredient.
